plan.strategy: Establish the authoritative baseline for the unmodified best-so-far SELU in-place seed
plan.code_changes: None; seed copied byte-identically from the provided best-so-far source
plan.hypothesis: The seed's per-dtype UB block sizing (16384 fp16 / 8192 else), direct-launch fast path and full-stride generic kernel reproduce the parent measurements; per-workload latencies reveal whether large cases are vector-bound (exp) or launch-bound

expected_effect.mechanism: No change; records per-workload latency and speedup decomposition for all 12 timing cases

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline decomposition: 9 of 12 timing workloads are host-launch-bound (18.2-19.1us vs reference 12.6-14.1us, speedups 0.71-0.74); the three large ones are device-bound with 1.246x (fp16 16M), 0.709x (bf16 16M) and 0.596x (fp32 16M).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement to compare. Measured means on device (bounded debug probes, same session): full call 14.0us for 1024 elements of which the compiled launcher's C call is ~9.4-10.2us and Python work ~3.5us (stream get 0.62, address wrapper 0.57, numel/data_ptr/dict/contiguity ~1.0, call frames ~1.5), while torch.selu_ is 7.4-9.0us. On the 16M cases the device body is ~70us (fp32), of which a pure copy is already ~64us at ~2 TB/s; a persistent grid-stride copy reached 46us, so per-program tile overhead (not arithmetic) is the large-case limiter.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the kernel math identical and cut host work per call: cache the compiled launcher primitives keyed by data pointer, verify dtype/numel/contiguity, and invoke the generated launcher directly with the current bare integer address (confirmed accepted and numerically correct on target) and current stream, dropping the int-subclass address wrapper and one Python frame.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Measuring through the standard Triton entry (53us) hides device time; only the direct launcher path gives a usable device-time comparison. Also grid must be a tuple, and driver.active.get_current_stream returns a raw int on this build, so the candidate's own _resolve_stream accessor must be used for stream reads.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline established with per-workload latency decomposition; conclusions drawn from bounded target probes rather than from aggregate ratios.

plan.strategy: Cut per-call host overhead by invoking the compiled launcher directly with a bare integer address from a single fast-path frame
plan.code_changes: Cache (dtype, numel, masked, launcher.launch, grid, function, packed_metadata, stream_getter) keyed by data_ptr; fast path verifies contiguity/dtype/numel then calls the generated launcher inline with the current bare integer address and current stream. The int-subclass address wrapper and the inner launch closure frame are gone; masked/strided/unaligned/debug paths unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The nine small timing workloads are host-launch-bound at ~18.5us, of which ~3.5us is Python-side work measured directly on target (address wrapper 0.57us, stream 0.62us, numel/data_ptr/dict/contiguity 1.0us, extra frame); eliminating the wrapper object and the inner closure frame will raise every small-case speedup from ~0.73 to ~0.83

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes ~2.3us of per-call Python from the measured path (address object 0.57us, wrapper frame ~1.5us, tuple key) while keeping the same 9.4us compiled launcher, so the nine launch-bound workloads should move from ~18.5us toward ~16us

conclusion.root_cause: Per-call Python work dominated the nine small workloads; eliminating the int-subclass address construction and the intermediate launch closure frame brought the measured full call from ~18.5us to ~13.4us while the device body stayed identical.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted ~2.3us of removable Python per call; observed 18.5 -> 13.4us (about 5.1us) on all nine small cases, so the expectation was exceeded. Aggregate 0.7527 -> 0.8632. Per workload: small cases 0.7395/0.7137/0.7214/0.7371/0.7409/0.7416/0.7298/0.7426/0.7514 -> 0.8695/0.8832/0.9017/0.8926/0.8922/0.8930/0.8977/0.8582/0.8499; timing-3 unchanged 1.246 -> 1.250; timing-7 unchanged 0.709 -> 0.710; timing-11 unchanged 0.596 -> 0.598, i.e. the device body was untouched as intended. Remaining gap on small cases is the compiled launcher call itself (~9.4us, confirmed by direct measurement) against a reference at ~11.7us.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The nine launch-bound cases are now within ~1.7us of the reference and the remaining host work is the compiled launcher itself (~9.4us) plus irreducible metadata reads, so switch to the large cases: give the three 16M contiguous workloads a persistent grid-stride SELU kernel (grid = num_vectorcore, current dtype block, num_stages=1 so the tile still fits UB) to cut per-program tile overhead.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The direct-launcher path is only cheap if the surrounding Python is cheap too: removing the int-subclass address object and the inner closure frame cut much more (5.1us) than the isolated probe costs suggested, because the closed-over stream/address/defaults were re-evaluated down two Python frames per call.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Baseline identified host launch overhead as the dominant aggregate lever; the host fast-path rewrite realized it, so the remaining budget goes to the three device-bound large cases.

plan.strategy: Persistent grid-stride kernel for long contiguous tensors to cut per-program overhead on the three large timing workloads
plan.code_changes: Added _selu_persist(X, TILES, G, BLOCK) grid-stride kernel; for contiguous inputs with n % block == 0 and tiles >= 4 * num_vectorcore the entry binds this kernel with grid=num_vectorcore and num_stages=1 (falls back to the plain tile grid if that compile fails). Host fast path, masked, strided and fallback paths unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: On the 16M cases the device body is limited by per-program tile cost rather than arithmetic (a pure copy at the same tile size costs 78us vs 83us for the full SELU), and a persistent grid-stride kernel measured 73.9us vs 83.0us for f32 and 75.5us vs 83.8us for bf16 with grid=num_vectorcore

expected_effect.mechanism: Replaces ~1024-2048 short-lived programs with one program per vector core looping over the same dtype-sized tiles, removing the per-program setup cost that dominates the 16M cases

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker (4/4 workloads: selu_-timing-11, selu_-timing-7, selu_-timing-3, selu_-timing-0). The service declared capabilities performance_counters, pipeline_utilization, kernel_profile and instruction_listing, but every result returned an empty capability set, an empty artifact list and no metrics, so no artifact could be cited as evidence.

conclusion.root_cause: The 16M workloads were limited by per-program tile overhead rather than arithmetic; one persistent program per vector core looping over the same dtype-sized tiles removed 8-10us of device time while keeping the tile inside the UB budget via num_stages=1.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted ~+2.7% aggregate from ~10% device gains on the three large cases; observed 0.8632 -> 0.8871 (+2.8%). Per workload: timing-3 1.250 -> 1.359 (45.6 -> 41.9us), timing-7 0.710 -> 0.783 (83.3 -> 75.5us), timing-11 0.598 -> 0.677 (82.7 -> 72.9us); the nine launch-bound cases stayed in the same 11.6-13.1us band (0.82-0.94, reference timing itself drifted down to 9.6-11.8us). The gains match the probe prediction almost exactly (probe: f32 83.0 -> 73.9us, bf16 83.8 -> 75.5us, f16 46.4 -> 42.3us). Remaining gap: fp32 16M is still 1.48x off the reference and a measured persistent copy floor of ~60us for the same traffic bounds further pure-kernel improvement to ~13us.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The persistent path is bound at one program per vector core (G = num_vectorcore, num_stages=1). The next experiment should test 2 programs per vector core (grid = 2 * num_vectorcore, which needs no extra UB) and, independently, routing the 1M-element workloads through the persistent path, since bf16 16M still trails the reference at 0.783 and the fp32 16M copy floor (~60us measured) leaves ~13us of headroom.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Per-program tile cost, not arithmetic, dominated the 16M cases: an identical-tile pure copy cost 78us of 83us, so the winning change was program granularity (one program per vector core with an in-program loop over the same tiles) rather than reducing vector ops; exp2 and fp16-negative-branch variants were measured and were slower or UB-infeasible.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Host overhead was the first lever (round 2, +14.7% aggregate); after it was exhausted, the large-case device structure became the limiter and program granularity delivered the remaining measured gain.
